description: Hop on one leg, stiff ankles, and count. The ankle hop test exposes the truth about your ankle tendons: whether they return energy or eat it. Here is the forty-hop line, the ground-contact science, and the bounce protocol that rebuilds your spring.

lines: Each hop is a spring landing
and a spring launch, back to back.
beats.title: NO REST FOR THE SPRING

scenes.narration: Stand on one leg, hands on your hips. Now hop. Small, quick hops, straight up and down on the same spot, and here is the rule that makes this a tendon test: your heel never touches the ground, and your knee barely bends. All the work happens at the ankle. Count how many clean hops you can do in a row before the rhythm breaks, the heel drops, or you start traveling across the floor. Test both legs. That count is your ankle hop score, and it tells the truth about your ankle tendons in a way no other test on this channel does. A calf raise lets the tendon rest between reps. A jump uses it once. Hopping chains the spring landing to launch, landing to launch, with no pause to hide in, and it asks one question forty times in a row: does this tendon return energy, or does it eat it? Every hop that gets lower and heavier is a hop where the answer changed. Keep your number, both legs. At the end of this video I will tell you exactly what it reveals about your ankle tendons, and it is not what your calf size suggests.

scenes.label: THE LINE BETWEEN LEAKING AND LAUNCHING
scenes.narration: Here is the line. Forty clean single-leg hops, heel up, rhythm unbroken, is where normal ankles become wired ankles. Under fifteen hops, the tendon is leaking energy on every contact, and each landing costs the muscle more than the last. Fifteen to forty means the spring is learning to recycle, and your count will climb quickly once you train the rhythm. Over eighty hops per leg, you are in sprinter and jumper territory, where the ankle barely thinks of the ground as an obstacle. Be honest about what counts. A hop where the heel slaps down is a failed hop wearing a costume, and a hop where the knee does the work is a squat jump in disguise. The tendon only gets graded when it does the job alone.
scenes.sub: under 15: leaking - 15 to 40: building - over 80: sprinter grade

lines: Too fast for new muscle force.
The tendon pays or the hop dies.
beats.title: NO TIME TO PUSH

scenes.narration: Understand what a hop actually is, because it is stranger than it looks. When you land, your foot is on the ground for about a fifth of a second. In that blink, your body weight multiplies, your Achilles stretches under the load, and then you are airborne again. There is no time in a fifth of a second for your calf muscle to build new force from scratch. Muscle is simply too slow. So the hop is paid for almost entirely by the tendon, which stored the landing energy and fires it back like a spring being released. Hop after hop, the same transaction repeats: stretch, store, fire. If the tendon is stiff and well organized, it returns most of what it borrowed and the rhythm feels free. If it is soft or disorganized, it returns less each time, the muscle has to cover the difference, and within fifteen hops the muscle is bankrupt. That bankruptcy is the moment your rhythm broke. Your count is a direct audit of the spring, with no accountant tricks available.

The number that governs all of this is energy return. A healthy, trained Achilles gives back the large majority of the energy it absorbs, which is why elite hoppers and sprinters look like they are bouncing on something hidden. An untrained tendon returns far less. The missing energy does not vanish politely. It turns into heat and extra muscle work, and you feel it as hops that get lower, louder, and more desperate. This is also why two guys with identical calf raises can be forty hops apart. The calf raise tests how much force the system can produce slowly. The hop test audits how much energy the system keeps at speed. Different exam, different subject. And here is the hopeful science: energy return improves with training on two timelines. The rhythm and timing improve in weeks, as your nervous system learns the bounce. The tendon structure improves in months, as slow heavy work rebuilds the spring itself. Train both, and the count climbs on both clocks at once.

beats.text: THE QUIET LEG IS THE RISK

scenes.narration: Now compare your legs, because hopping is ruthless about asymmetry. In a calf raise you can cheat a weak side with tempo and grit. In a hop chain there is nowhere to hide: the weak ankle lands softer, stays on the ground longer, and returns less, and you can hear it before you can see it. One side sounds like a drum, tight and quick. The other sounds like a thud. That thud is the sound of energy being eaten. Clinicians care about this gap for a hard reason. The leg with the leaking spring is the leg that lands badly when you are tired, and tired landings are where ankles roll and knees complain. If your counts differ by more than about a third, the quiet leg becomes the priority, exactly like the balance and calf tests taught. Train it first, train it fresh, and let the strong leg wait its turn. Symmetry is not vanity. On one leg, at speed, symmetry is safety equipment.

beats.label: MORE HOPS BEFORE THE SPRING TIRES

scenes.narration: Your advantage in this test is the same one the spring keeps handing you. Every hop loads the ankle tendons with your body weight, multiplied. A lighter body means a smaller multiplication, a cooler tendon, and a muscle that can cover the spring's losses for far longer before going bankrupt. Heavy guys often start hopping impressively and fall apart by hop twenty, because each of their landings costs more than yours does. You are built for the long chain. It is no accident that the athletes who hop, skip, and bound for a living, sprinters, jumpers, court players, carry as little non-working mass as they can get away with. The hop test is where the skinny build stops apologizing. Your low number today is not a verdict on your frame. It is a receipt showing your spring has never been trained at speed, and springs trained at speed on light frames improve embarrassingly fast.
Now hop with me. One leg, stiff ankle, heel floating. Twenty seconds per leg, forty rest, three rounds. Small, quick, quiet. Go.

Here is your week. Three days a week, hop training while you are fresh: three sets of fifteen to twenty seconds per leg, full rest between sets, every landing quiet. Fresh matters more than volume here, because tired hops teach the spring to leak. On the other days, the slow road: heavy calf raises and heel drops, which rebuild the structure the hops are testing. Three mistakes stall this count. Hopping on a sore Achilles, which turns training into damage, so if tendon pain shows up and persists, stop the hops and see a professional before resuming. Bending the knee to survive the set, which quietly moves the exam from the ankle to the thigh. And chasing huge daily volumes, when tendons want small, perfect doses with days to rebuild between them. Quiet landings or stop. That rule alone will carry your count further than any amount of suffering.

scenes.label: RETEST DAY - BOTH LEGS, SAME FLOOR
scenes.narration: So, your count. Under fifteen per leg: the spring is leaking, and leaking springs on light frames are the fastest fix in this season. Fifteen to forty: you are building, and your job is fresh hops for rhythm and slow raises for structure. Over forty with a small gap between legs: your ankles are wired, and every step you take is partly free. Put both numbers in the comments, left and right. Just the numbers. We retest in thirty days, same floor, same rules, heels up, and we listen for the thud to disappear.
scenes.sub: under 15: leaking - 15 to 40: building - over 40 even: wired

scenes.narration: Thirty days from now, same floor, both legs, and we count what the spring returns. Subscribe, because next we shrink the push-up down to a diamond and interrogate the tendon behind your elbow. This is {channel}. Train the cable.

title: Your Ankle Hop Test Reveals the Truth About Your ankle tendons
